name: Čert
description: The shaggy, chain-rattling devil who walks the Czech streets with St Nicholas and an angel on 5 December

debut.title: Czech and Slovak folk tradition
debut.era: an old figure of folk tales, and of the St Nicholas visit on 5 December

legend: On the evening of 5 December, the eve of St Nicholas Day, three figures go from door to door in Czech and Slovak towns: Mikuláš, the saint in his bishop's robes, an angel in white, and a čert, a devil. Mikuláš asks each child whether they've been good, and many recite a poem or sing a song to prove it. The angel hands out sweets and fruit. The čert, with his horns, blackened face, shaggy fur and rattling chains, is there for the others: a lump of coal or a potato, and the threat of a ride to hell in his sack. Outside this one night he is a stock character of Czech fairy tales, where he is more often foolish than frightening, and is regularly outwitted by a sharp-tongued villager.

myths.claim: The čert comes on Christmas Eve.
myths.explanation: His night is 5 December, the eve of St Nicholas Day.

myths.claim: He walks with an angel as well as the saint.
myths.explanation: The visiting party is three: Mikuláš, an angel and a devil.

myths.claim: In Czech fairy tales the devil always wins.
myths.explanation: He usually loses. The čert of the folk tales is easily tricked, and often sent packing.

myths.claim: Dvořák wrote an opera about a čert.
myths.explanation: The Devil and Kate (Čert a Káča) opened at the National Theatre in Prague in 1899.

powers: A sack with room for one more
Making a whole street of children suddenly polite
weaknesses: The angel standing next to him
Anyone cleverer than he is, which is most people
legacy: Antonín Dvořák's comic opera The Devil and Kate (1899)
The Mikuláš evening, still kept on 5 December across the Czech Republic and Slovakia
